newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine sees woeful grain crop but will export.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine sees woeful grain crop but will export.

text.p: Ukraine, once the breadbasket of Eastern Europe but now the distressed producer of a pitiful grain harvest, said on Thursday it would get by without imports and even export some of its crop.
"A very difficult harvest year is almost finished and we will gather 26 million tonnes of grain," Deputy Prime Minister for Agriculture Mykhailo Zubets told a news conference.
"We do not need to import any grain this year."
Instead, Ukraine would export three million tonnes, mostly of winter wheat, he said.
Ukraine's disastrous grain harvest this year is half of 1990 output and a full 10 million tonnes below last year's harvest.
Officials had originally predicted 1996 output of 38 million tonnes, but revised forecasts down after drought damaged crops.
Zubets' forecast was a notch up from previous forecasts of 25 million tonnes.
But it still reflects a crisis in Ukrainian agriculture, once the pride of the Soviet Union.
The harvest, which is nearly over, comes as the country struggles to cast off its Soviet past, which is still deeply embedded in its inefficient collective farms.
Shortages of fertiliser, herbicides, fuel, tractors, spare parts and silos means that waste and losses are rife.
"This year it (the grain harvest) was low quality," said one Western trader, who put Ukraine's maximum domestic annual requirements at 12 million tonnes.
Government sources have said the former Soviet republic needs about 10 million tonnes a year to meet demand to feed its people and livestock.
Ukraine traditionally exports to Russia, Central Asia and Eastern Europe.
"Their yield production was far less this year, and half of 1990," said a Western agricultural specialist, commenting on the quality of the harvest.
"But for domestic needs they should have adequate supplies for food for people and feed for livestock."
Still, grain quality was so poor that Ukraine was accepting class five wheat, normally reserved for animal feed, as a substitute for class three wheat, used for making bread, he added.
Kiev, struggling through economic reforms, has no cash for expensive grain imports.
Domestic consumption has fallen, and livestock numbers have dwindled as farmers find it cheaper to slaughter cattle than to feed them.
Zubets said the government had ordered an additional half million hectares sown to winter wheat this autumn and that officials hoped for output of 40 million tonnes of grain next year.
But such a target could be unreachable unless more effective farming methods are used.
In a sign that changes may be a long way off, the government last week threw its support behind the collective farm system, saying it lacked enough cash to back the few private farmers Ukraine has.
